title: Anointing the sick
hook: oil and prayer for the sick (James 5:14)

segments.voice: Yesterday, ordination: hands laid on with prayer, and teachers sent away. Your line was hands laid on.

A small metal case, the size of a lipstick. Inside, a pad of cotton soaked in olive oil. A priest carries it in a jacket pocket down a hospital corridor, into a room where a man lies with a drip in his arm. Across the city, a grocery-store bottle of olive oil sits on a coffee table. A few friends from church gather around a woman in an armchair. One puts a dab of oil on her forehead with a thumb, and they begin to pray. Different rooms, the same two things. Today's word is unction.

Day one hundred fifty-four paired confession with healing oil; today, the oil. Unction means an anointing with oil, and for the sick the instructions come from James: "Is any sick among you? let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord: And the prayer of faith shall save the sick, and the Lord shall raise him up; and if he have committed sins, they shall be forgiven him." The sick person calls. The church comes. Oil and prayer go together. First, the oil was ordinary. In Mark, the disciples anoint "with oil many that were sick, and healed them." The Good Samaritan bandages a stranger's wounds, "pouring in oil and wine." James puts that kitchen-shelf remedy inside a prayer. Catholics call it the anointing of the sick and count it a sacrament. Once called extreme unction and kept mostly for the dying, it's now offered to anyone facing serious illness, surgery, or the frailty of age. The Orthodox call it Holy Unction, and in some parishes people who aren't bedridden at all come forward to be anointed during Holy Week. Some Protestant churches anoint with oil when elders pray for the sick; others lay hands on the sick and pray without it. Last, the promise: the Lord shall raise him up. Some Christians read that as bodily healing; others hear strength, forgiveness, and company in suffering. Some recover and some don't. The rite says they're not left alone.

Bring to mind one person who is ill right now, in a hospital, at home, or sick in a way nobody can see, and sit as you would in a chair pulled up beside them. If you pray, ask God to raise them up, in whatever way that means for them today. If you don't, keep them company in your mind, the way the elders in James came when called.
Unction. An anointing with oil. For the sick, it's oil and prayer together, brought by the church when someone calls, as in James.
Your line: oil and prayer. The sick call, and the church comes. Day one thousand three hundred forty-eight.

howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the anointing of the sick as a sacrament for those seriously ill or frail with age; the Orthodox celebrate Holy Unction, in some parishes for all the faithful during Holy Week; some Protestant churches anoint with oil when elders pray for the sick, and others lay on hands and pray.

Original note: εὐχέλαιον combines εὐχή (prayer) and ἔλαιον (oil). This is a compound name, flagged here under the etymology rule; confirm spelling and the note.
